chunks: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the person in ihram: does he break his teeth (with a toothpick)? He said, 'Yes, there is no harm in it.' I said to him, 'What about eating the citric fruit (utrujj)?' He said, 'Yes.' I said to him, 'For it has a pleasant scent,' so he said, 'The citric fruit is food, and it is not among the perfumes.'

Because he only permitted its eating and did not say that it is permissible for him to smell it, and the first report is detailed, so acting upon it is preferable. Al-Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And he does not perform cupping, nor breaks his teeth, unless he fears destruction to himself.

key_terms.اَلطِّيبُ: Perfume/scent (specifically the scent used for grooming, distinct from food scent)
key_terms.اَلْمُحْرِمُ: The person in the state of ihram (ritual consecration for Hajj or Umrah)
key_terms.يَتَخَلَّلُ: To break the teeth (using a toothpick or similar tool)

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible for a person in ihram to eat citrus fruits or use their scent?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) distinguishes between the permissibility of consuming utrujj (citrus fruit) as food and the prohibition of its scent as perfume, illustrating the Shia scholarly principle of applying specific permissions literally while maintaining general prohibitions. This nuance highlights the juristic rigor in distinguishing between ingestion and olfactory use during ihram. The hadith further clarifies that medical procedures like cupping are forbidden unless necessity (darura) dictates otherwise to preserve life.
